title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

reading.body:
State Farm's defense lawyers used a generative AI tool called Irys to draft legal filings in a lawsuit over fire and water damage to a home in Carson, California. The tool generated false case citations, nonexistent legal holdings, and fabricated quotations. The lawyers relied on the AI to catch errors in citations and did not independently verify the cases before submitting the filings to court.

This is a failure of verification at deployment. A system designed to assist with legal research was used without human review of its factual claims, which is the minimum requirement for any AI tool producing citations in legal documents. The tool did not flag its own errors, and the lawyers did not apply professional standards of checking case law before filing. Catching this would have required either the legal team to verify citations against legal databases before filing, or a policy explicitly requiring human review of all AI-generated case references.

It is not established whether the false citations affected the substantive outcome of the case or what consequences the state bar or court imposed.

reports.title: State Farm defense lawyers admit AI generated fake cases in LA lawsuit
AI hallucinated case law in insurance company’s filings in L.A. County house fire dispute
AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

summary:
State Farm's defense lawyers apologized for using artificial intelligence that generated fake legal cases, nonexistent quotes, and false legal holdings in court filings for a lawsuit involving a Los Angeles homeowner. The homeowner, Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, sued State Farm and others after a 2020 fire destroyed her Carson home and subsequent water damage during repairs prevented completion of reconstruction work. She claims delays in getting State Farm's approval for repairs led to financial ruin, including bankruptcy and foreclosure.

Lawyer Jacquelene Robinson admitted she used an AI tool called Irys to help prepare motions, believing it would catch citation errors, when it did not. She confirmed seven case citations across eight filings did not exist, along with incorrect case titles and fabricated quotes. Lead counsel Kenneth Katel apologized and accepted responsibility, stating the firm has updated its AI policies. The trial is scheduled for October 2025, and the discovery highlights a growing problem as 41 percent of law firms now use generative AI, with over 1,900 documented legal hallucinations recorded globally.
